questions.question: Which statement best characterizes domain-specific accelerators compared to general-purpose GPUs?
questions.choice_A: They specialize hardware datapaths and memory hierarchies for a narrow set of workloads, trading off generality for higher efficiency.
questions.choice_B: They are always more energy efficient than CPUs across all workloads due to higher clock speeds.
questions.choice_C: They rely primarily on out-of-order superscalar execution to hide memory latency.
questions.choice_D: They avoid on-chip memory to reduce die area and emphasize off-chip bandwidth.

questions.question: When comparing energy cost models of arithmetic, which is typically true at modern technology nodes?
questions.choice_A: A 32-bit floating-point add usually consumes less energy than an 8-bit integer multiply.
questions.choice_B: Memory access to off-chip DRAM generally dominates the energy cost relative to on-chip arithmetic operations.
questions.choice_C: All adds and multiplies have similar energy regardless of bit-width due to voltage scaling.
questions.choice_D: Energy costs of arithmetic are largely independent of operand precision once pipelined.

questions.question: Why do systolic arrays improve both performance and energy efficiency for dense linear algebra?
questions.choice_A: They reduce the number of operations by computing approximate results.
questions.choice_B: They broadcast operands from DRAM to all PEs directly, minimizing on-chip movement.
questions.choice_C: They exploit data reuse through local, regular communication, keeping data stationary and reducing long-distance transfers.
questions.choice_D: They execute instructions out-of-order to improve ALU utilization.

questions.question: Which factor most constrains sustained throughput on memory-bound workloads on accelerators?
questions.choice_A: Peak arithmetic operations per second (TOPS/TFLOPS).
questions.choice_B: Off-chip memory bandwidth and the ability to reuse data in on-chip SRAM.
questions.choice_C: Instruction cache size for control flow heavy kernels.
questions.choice_D: Thermal design power when operating below nominal voltage.

questions.question: In an energy model, which component is most likely to be underestimated if only compute operations are counted?
questions.choice_A: Dynamic power of ALUs executing multiplies.
questions.choice_B: Leakage power in registers during idle cycles.
questions.choice_C: Energy of data movement across the memory hierarchy, especially DRAM accesses.
questions.choice_D: Clock distribution power in the compute core.

questions.question: How do TPUs differ architecturally from traditional GPUs for ML workloads?
questions.choice_A: TPUs emphasize large systolic arrays for dense matrix multiply and on-chip buffers tuned for tensor reuse.
questions.choice_B: TPUs prioritize graphics pipeline stages to accelerate rasterization and shading.
questions.choice_C: TPUs eliminate SIMD/SIMT execution entirely in favor of scalar cores.
questions.choice_D: TPUs rely on speculative execution and branch prediction as their primary performance feature.

questions.question: What is a key design trade-off when increasing on-chip SRAM capacity in an accelerator?
questions.choice_A: Larger SRAM always reduces energy because it allows more data reuse without side effects.
questions.choice_B: Increased SRAM capacity can reduce DRAM traffic but may increase access energy per read/write and lengthen wire distances.
questions.choice_C: SRAM capacity does not affect die area because memory compilers are area-neutral.
questions.choice_D: More SRAM reduces latency variability by increasing off-chip bandwidth.

questions.question: Which statement about integer vs floating-point arithmetic is generally accurate for accelerator design?
questions.choice_A: Integer operations are always slower due to lack of hardware support.
questions.choice_B: Low-precision integer arithmetic (e.g., 8-bit) often delivers higher throughput and lower energy than 32-bit floating point for tolerant workloads.
questions.choice_C: Floating-point operations are more energy efficient because they avoid normalization.
questions.choice_D: Switching to integer arithmetic does not change memory bandwidth requirements.

questions.question: Why is DRAM-to-SRAM data transfer particularly costly in energy models?
questions.choice_A: DRAM operations have negligible activation overhead but high compute cost.
questions.choice_B: The physical distance and I/O drivers required for off-chip communication make each DRAM access orders of magnitude more energy-intensive than on-chip accesses.
questions.choice_C: SRAM requires precharge and refresh, increasing transfer cost.
questions.choice_D: DRAM reads reduce static power more than writes increase it.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of Local Processing Units (LPUs) or similar near-memory compute units?
questions.choice_A: To offload control flow to the CPU while keeping data on the GPU.
questions.choice_B: To perform computation close to where data resides, reducing data movement and associated energy.
questions.choice_C: To increase DRAM frequency to match compute frequency.
questions.choice_D: To convert floating-point data to fixed-point during I/O.

questions.question: When estimating energy across designs, why is roofline analysis often complemented with operational intensity profiling?
questions.choice_A: Roofline alone precisely predicts latency but not throughput.
questions.choice_B: Operational intensity determines where a workload sits relative to compute and bandwidth ceilings, guiding whether to optimize arithmetic or data movement.
questions.choice_C: Operational intensity is only needed for GPU kernels with divergent control flow.
questions.choice_D: Roofline models ignore memory bandwidth entirely.

questions.question: Which scenario best illustrates off-chip bandwidth bottleneck implications?
questions.choice_A: A kernel with extremely high data reuse that fits entirely in on-chip SRAM.
questions.choice_B: A streaming inference pipeline with low reuse where activations and weights are repeatedly fetched from DRAM, limiting achieved TOPS despite abundant ALUs.
questions.choice_C: A compute-bound GEMM executed on a large systolic array.
questions.choice_D: A kernel dominated by register-to-register operations.

questions.question: What is a common pitfall when comparing energy efficiency across different accelerators using only 'TOPS/W'?
questions.choice_A: TOPS/W inherently penalizes low-precision arithmetic.
questions.choice_B: It conflates arithmetic capability with memory system efficiency and may not reflect workload-specific operational intensity or precision requirements.
questions.choice_C: It ignores leakage power at advanced nodes where dynamic power is negligible.
questions.choice_D: It cannot be measured on ASICs.

questions.question: In an energy cost model that separates compute and memory, which intervention most directly reduces the memory energy term without changing arithmetic counts?
questions.choice_A: Increasing pipeline depth of the ALUs.
questions.choice_B: Reordering loops to maximize data reuse and tile into on-chip buffers.
questions.choice_C: Raising the clock frequency to reduce execution time.
questions.choice_D: Using double-precision arithmetic to improve numerical stability.

questions.question: Which architectural feature of GPUs primarily targets latency hiding for memory-bound kernels?
questions.choice_A: Large reorder buffers and speculative execution.
questions.choice_B: Massive multithreading with warp scheduling to switch to ready warps while others stall.
questions.choice_C: Dedicated fixed-function matrix engines without caches.
questions.choice_D: Clock gating based on branch prediction.

questions.question: How does reducing numeric precision impact both compute and memory subsystems in practice?
questions.choice_A: It only affects compute units; memory traffic remains constant.
questions.choice_B: It lowers per-operation energy and may increase throughput while also reducing memory footprint and bandwidth demand, often shifting the roofline position.
questions.choice_C: It decreases DRAM activation energy but increases on-chip wire energy.
questions.choice_D: It increases cache miss rates because smaller types fragment lines.

questions.question: Which method provides a credible basis for cross-design energy comparisons when RTL or silicon is unavailable?
questions.choice_A: Using peak frequency as a proxy for energy per operation.
questions.choice_B: Analytical modeling calibrated with published microbenchmarks (e.g., per-op and per-byte energies) and validated against known kernels.
questions.choice_C: Extrapolating from unrelated benchmarks on older process nodes.
questions.choice_D: Assuming linear scaling from FPGA to ASIC without adjustment.

questions.question: In a systolic array for matrix multiply, which dataflow choice most reduces on-chip traffic for weights?
questions.choice_A: Output-stationary: keep partial sums stationary while streaming both inputs and weights each cycle.
questions.choice_B: Weight-stationary: keep weights in place and stream inputs, accumulating partial sums locally or nearby.
questions.choice_C: Input-stationary: keep inputs stationary and stream weights and partial sums.
questions.choice_D: Random-stationary: randomly pin either inputs or weights per cycle.

questions.question: What is a practical implication of the 'bytes-per-op' ratio in energy modeling?
questions.choice_A: If bytes-per-op exceeds the machine balance (BW/OPS), the kernel is likely compute-bound.
questions.choice_B: Lower bytes-per-op generally indicates better potential to be compute-bound and lower energy per result due to amortized memory costs.
questions.choice_C: Bytes-per-op is irrelevant when caches are present.
questions.choice_D: Higher bytes-per-op always improves energy efficiency by utilizing memory bandwidth.

questions.question: Which consideration is most important when claiming energy benefits of near-memory compute (e.g., LPUs) over traditional accelerators?
questions.choice_A: Ensuring the compute units have higher peak TFLOPS.
questions.choice_B: Quantifying reduced off-chip and on-package data movement in the full system context, including any overheads for coherence and control.
questions.choice_C: Matching the instruction set architecture to x86 for software compatibility.
questions.choice_D: Using double buffering to increase arithmetic intensity in the core.

questions.question: When modeling energy for integer vs floating-point pipelines, which factor is commonly overlooked?
questions.choice_A: The presence of multiply-add fusion in floating point.
questions.choice_B: Control logic energy dominating at high utilization.
questions.choice_C: Format conversion and quantization/dequantization overheads, which can erode the gains of low-precision integer compute.
questions.choice_D: Branch predictor training costs in ML inference.
